metadata.title: Why Three Reasonable Fairness Definitions Cannot All Be True
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: why three reasonable fairness definitions cannot all be true simultaneously. Lands the carry-out that calibrating scores across groups with different base rates forces their error rates apart — the conflict is Bayes' rule, not a tooling gap.
metadata.anchor_pair: B06 -> B07 (The odds identity balance v/(1-v) = p/(1-p) * t/f linking precision, base rate, and error-rate ratio)
metadata.one_flag: B10 — the two degenerate mathematical escapes (equal base rates or zero errors) never hold in social deployments
metadata.mirror_pair: B11 / B12 — mirrored construction (both directions: calibration ⇏ equal error rates, equal error rates ⇏ calibrated scores)

beats.narration_text: When an algorithm's scores mean the exact same thing across groups, we assume its error rates can be made equal too. But a four-line theorem from Bayes' rule proves they cannot. Let's trace why.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types naive question, hesitates on "be equal across groups?", corrects to "diverge across groups?"

props.text:
If an AI model has calibrated scores,
shouldn't its error rates
be equal across groups?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per course-skepticism SKILL.md. Liam reads over typing animation.

beats.narration_text: In 2016, journalists reported that the COMPAS risk tool had unequal false-positive rates across racial groups; its maker proved its scores were calibrated. Both were mathematically correct.

shot.new_visual_element: Two opposing audit claims on same model: Diverging False Positives vs Calibrated Risk Scores; Both Arithmetically Correct

production_viz.label: The Canonical Public Dispute
production_viz.mechanic: Split card: ProPublica audit vs Northpointe audit; both mathematically accurate.

beats.narration_text: The maker checked calibration parity: when the model assigns a risk score of seventy percent, exactly seventy percent of defendants in every group go on to reoffend. The score is honest.

shot.new_visual_element: Definition 1: Calibration Parity / Predictive Parity Card

production_viz.label: Definition 1: Calibration Parity
production_viz.mechanic: P(Outcome | Score = s, Group A) = P(Outcome | Score = s, Group B) = s. Score honesty.

beats.narration_text: The critics checked equalized odds: innocent people should face the same low false-positive rate, and guilty people should face the same true-positive rate, regardless of group. Error costs are shared equally.

shot.new_visual_element: Definitions 2 & 3: Equalized Odds (FPR Parity & TPR Parity)

production_viz.label: Definitions 2 & 3: Equalized Odds
production_viz.mechanic: Equal False-Positive Rate (innocents) and Equal True-Positive Rate (guilty). Equal distribution of error costs.

beats.narration_text: The natural assumption is that one side made an engineering error, collected bad data, or used a biased loss function that better tooling could fix. But no algorithm can satisfy both.

shot.new_visual_element: The Tooling Fallacy Struck: Bad Data or Algorithmic Flaw? Struck through with Terracotta

production_viz.label: Wrong Guess: The Tooling Fallacy
production_viz.mechanic: Hypothesis: Bad Data / Buggy Loss Function. Struck out: Arithmetic impossibility, not tooling defect.

beats.narration_text: To see why, write down Bayes' rule. In any group with positive base rate p, true-positive rate t, and false-positive rate f, the positive predictive value v is precision: the probability a positive score is real.

shot.new_visual_element: Bayes' Rule Definitions: p (base rate), t (TPR), f (FPR), v (precision / PPV)

production_viz.label: The Four Bayes Quantities
production_viz.mechanic: Definition card displaying p, t, f, and precision v = p*t / (p*t + (1-p)*f).

beats.narration_text: Rearrange Bayes' rule into odds form. The precision odds equal the base-rate odds multiplied by the error-rate ratio: v over one minus v equals p over one minus p, times t over f.

shot.new_visual_element: Visual Object: The Odds Identity Balance in equilibrium: v/(1-v) = p/(1-p) * t/f

production_viz.label: The Odds Identity Balance
production_viz.mechanic: Visual Object planted: Odds balance scale linking precision odds to base-rate odds and error-rate ratio.

beats.narration_text: Now put Group A and Group B side by side. Calibration requires the score to mean the same probability everywhere, fixing the precision ratio to one. Transform the balance: the error-rate ratio is tied directly to the base rates.

shot.new_visual_element: Manim Move: Transform. Two odds identities combined; precision ratio locked to 1.0; error ratio isolated against base rate ratio

production_viz.label: Transforming the Two-Group Balance
production_viz.mechanic: Kinetic transformation: Calibration locks left side to 1; error-rate ratio equals inverted base-rate odds ratio.

beats.narration_text: Whenever the base rates differ between groups, the base-rate term moves away from one. To preserve equality, the error-rate ratio t over f is mathematically forced to tilt in the opposite direction.

shot.new_visual_element: The Tilted Balance: Base-rate weight shifts away from 1.0; Error-rate side tilts sharply to compensate

production_viz.label: The Forced Tilt of Error Rates
production_viz.mechanic: Dynamic balance scale tilting: Divergent group base rates force the error rate ratio t/f apart.

beats.narration_text: Equalized odds demands equal true-positive rates and equal false-positive rates, forcing the error ratio to one. But with different base rates, that equality is impossible. One of the two fairness definitions must break.

shot.new_visual_element: Chouldechova's Impossibility Theorem: Contradiction Card between Error Parity and Calibration Parity

production_viz.label: The Four-Line Impossibility Theorem
production_viz.mechanic: Theorem card showing 1.0 = (Disparity Factor) * 1.0 contradiction. Mathematical proof complete.

beats.narration_text: One flag — the arithmetic allows exactly two escapes: identical base rates across all groups, or clairvoyant prediction with zero errors. In real-world social evaluations, neither escape ever happens.

shot.new_visual_element: The One Flag: The Two Theoretical Escapes (Identical Base Rates or Zero Errors) — Impossible in practice

production_viz.label: The One Flag: Two Degenerate Escapes
production_viz.mechanic: Card: 1. p_A = p_B (Equal Base Rates), 2. t = 1, f = 0 (Clairvoyant model). Neither holds in practice.

beats.narration_text: In one direction, proving your risk scores are perfectly calibrated across demographic groups does not mean error rates are fair. If base rates differ, calibrated scores guarantee unequal error rates.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction A: Calibrated Risk Scores do not imply Equal Error Rates

production_viz.label: Direction A: Calibration ≠ Equal Errors
production_viz.mechanic: Card: Honest scores across groups with unequal base rates guarantee unequal false-positive rates.

beats.narration_text: In the other direction, forcing error rates to match across groups with different base rates does not guarantee score honesty. It mathematically guarantees that identical scores mean different probabilities for different groups.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction B: Equal Error Rates do not imply Calibrated Risk Scores

production_viz.label: Direction B: Equal Errors ≠ Calibration
production_viz.mechanic: Card: Matching error rates across groups with unequal base rates breaks score calibration.

beats.narration_text: Calibrating scores across groups with different base rates forces their error rates apart — the conflict is Bayes' rule, not a tooling gap.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take a predictive model evaluated across demographic groups in your organization. Measure the base rate of the positive outcome in each group, and inspect both the false-positive rate and the positive predictive value. When the base rates differ, which definition of fairness did the team choose to satisfy — and who signed off on the definition that had to break? Liam, in for Bear.
